title: Router Build Plan
eyebrow: Build plan for approval · both designs approved, no code yet
approval: Build plan approved: router windows app

short.lead: This is how I will build both approved designs, the website and the Windows app, as one pull request from shared code. Sessions are grouped by project only. Every session card shows its context use, its account's 5-hour limit and its account's weekly limit. The app adds finding accounts, starting and resuming sessions, and picking the account with the most room.
short.hint: Tap an item to see what it creates and what it needs from you.
items: On the website, the site asks Edge or Chrome for permission to read each Claude folder you point it at, and remembers them for next time. The Windows app finds your folders itself.
On the website, pick each folder once. After that, it is one Allow tap per visit. In the Windows app, there is nothing to do here.
Sessions from every account land in the same project column. Each card has a small tag showing which folder (account) it came from.
Context comes straight from the session files. The 5-hour and weekly limits need the limit reporter, because Claude Code never saves them to a file.
If you want limits, tap Turn on limit tracking once for each account.
Each change merged into main republishes the site.
Turn on GitHub Pages in the repository settings, once.

Finds your Claude folders, resumes and starts sessions in Windows Terminal, marks active sessions, and picks the account with the most room for new ones. The installer is built on GitHub's Windows machines and attached to a GitHub Release.
Run the installer once, and click past the unsigned-app warning.
I build it as seven steps, each a GitHub issue, then open a pull request.
Pick your answer to each of the two questions in Your choices, then tap Copy my reply and send it.

What it is built with
A website, plus a separate Windows app that shows the same board.
A local app run by Node.js that you download and double-click.
The website is on GitHub Pages: you open a link in Edge or Chrome and nothing is downloaded. The Windows app is a separate installer.

A website can't read your files on its own. Edge and Chrome let a site read a folder you pick, after you allow it, so that is how this one sees your sessions. Firefox and Safari don't have this feature, so the site tells you to use Edge or Chrome.
chg
Accounts
Found from your folders. The site never renames or switches them.
Three slots named Main, Work and Spare, with an account picker for starting sessions.

Each account is a Claude folder (one you pick on the website, or one the app finds for you), shown by its own folder name, such as .claude-work. On the website, each card has a button that copies its resume command. In the app, Resume opens the session in a terminal, and the only account choice is when starting a new session, with the account that has the most room picked for you.

Your answer said accounts shouldn't split the board or be the way you switch, so the slot names are gone. Accounts show up as a tag on each card, and the Windows app also offers an account when you start a new session.
new
Limit reporter
Gets the 5-hour and weekly limits out of Claude Code.

Claude Code shows the limits only to its status line, the strip of text under the prompt. When you tap Turn on limit tracking for an account, the site saves a backup of that account's settings.json and then adds a small PowerShell reporter as its status line. Each time the status line updates, the reporter saves the numbers into the account folder for the site to read. If you already have a status line, the reporter runs it too, so its text still shows. Turn off limit tracking puts your backup back.
The limits are visible only inside each terminal, one session at a time.
Every session gets a saved reading of its account's limits.
You see every account's limits on one board, with the time each one resets.
new
First-run walkthrough
On the website, three skippable screens, starting with picking your folders. In the app, the first screen is a confirm list of the folders it found.

Screen one asks for your Claude folders and tells you where the usual one is. Screen two explains the colours and bars using your own projects. Screen three offers limit tracking. Skip takes you straight to the board.
There is no guide today.
A walkthrough that uses your real folders.
Setup takes one screen, and you can skip the rest.

Windows app
A Windows app (built with Electron) that shows the same board.

Finding accounts: every folder in your user folder named .claude or starting with .claude-. Resume: Windows Terminal opens in the project folder running claude --resume with that session, on its own account. New session: the account with the most room, meaning the lowest 5-hour use, is picked, and you can change it. Active: a session whose file changed in the last 2 minutes while Claude is running gets a green dot.
Only the website existed in the plan.
An installed app with the same board.
Setup is one confirm screen, and getting back into a project is one click.
new
Seven GitHub issues
The parent issue, Router prototype: a board of Claude Code sessions by project, as a website and a Windows app, has seven sub-issues.

The sub-issues are Folder access and session discovery, Board with context bars, Limit reporter and the Turn on limit tracking button, First-run walkthrough, Publish on GitHub Pages, Windows app: finding accounts, start and resume, active sessions, and Windows installer built on GitHub. Each one names what it depends on and when it is done.
No issues exist yet.
One issue per step.
You can see progress, and what blocks what, on GitHub.
choices: How should limit tracking be turned on?
One tap in the site, per account
The site backs up settings.json, adds the reporter, and keeps your existing status line working. Turn off limit tracking restores the backup.
Leave limits out of the prototype
Context bars only. The 5-hour and weekly bars come in a later version.
Option A gives you all three bars in the first version, and the backup means nothing is lost.
How should the shared code for the website and the Windows app be written?
No build step, so GitHub Pages serves the files as they are, and you can open any file and read it.
Catches more mistakes before they ship, but adds tooling and a build to every change.
Option A keeps the site small and easy to change, and the automated tests catch most of what TypeScript would.
